## **Previously on 201**
<br>
**tools** to figure out meanings in Semantics:<br><br>

### for two propositions <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> and <span style="color:blue"><b>q</b></span>:<br><br>

### <b><span style="color:deeppink">entailment</span></b>: a proposition <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> entails another proposition <span style="color:blue"><b>q</b></span> iff, whenever <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> is <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span>, <span style="color:blue"><b>q</b></span> must also be <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span><br><br>

### <b><span style="color:deeppink">presupposition</span></b>: a proposition <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> presupposes aother proposition <span style="color:blue"><b>q</b></span> iff both <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> and the <span style="color:orange"><b>negation</b></span> of <span style="color:green"><b>p</b></span> <b><span style="color:#CC0033">entail</span></b> <span style="color:blue"><b>q</b></span><br><br>

--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:deeppink">Set Theory</span></b></h3>
</div>

## **Set theory: Sets and Elements**
<br>
.pull-left[
a **set** is an abstract <u>collection of items</u>:<br><br>
- {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun} is the set of days of the week<br><br>

the individual items in a set are called **member**s or **element**s:<br><br>
- *Thursday* is a **member** or **element** of the set of days of the week<br><br>

The symbols <span style="color:green"><b>∈</b></span> and <span style="color:green"><b>∉</b></span> are used to specify whether an element is a member of a given set:<br><br>
  - *Mon* <span style="color:green"><b>∈</b></span> {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun}
  - *Oct* <span style="color:green"><b>∉</b></span> {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun}
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/1026/set.jpg" width="80%">
]

---
## **Set theory: Sets and Elements**
<br>
- as in other branches of mathematics, we can use variables to stand in for values:
.pull-left[
***A*** = {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun}
]
.pull-right[
defines variable ***A*** as the set of days
]
<br><br>

- by convention, we use **capital letters (*A*, *B*, *C*...)** for sets and <span style="color:green"><b>lowercase letters (<i>x</i>, <i>y</i>, <i>z</i>...)</b></span> for elements<br><br>

- we can first assign various elements to variables and then define sets based on them:
.pull-left[
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="color:#CC0033"><i><b>a</b></i></span> = Rutgers
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="color:green"><i><b>b</b></i></span> = Stanford
</div>
]
]
.pull-right[
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="color:deeppink"><i><b>c</b></i></span> = MIT
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="color:blue"><i><b>d</b></i></span> = Fudan
</div>
]
]
<br><br>
.pull-left[
  - ***U*** = {Rutgers, Stanford, MIT, Fudan}
]
.pull-right[
  - [[**U**niversities]]
]
.pull-left[
  - ***B*** = {Rutgers, Fudan}
]
.pull-right[
  - [[the **B**est Universities]]
] <br><br>
- we can also define sets in terms of their <span style="color:blue"><b>natural language meaning</b></span>
.pull-left[
  - ***D*** = [[days of the week]]
]
.pull-right[
  - [[Monday]] ∈ **D**
]<br><br>

- we put [[ ]] around natural language expressions to show we're talking about their meaning, not their structure, morphology, or sounds

---
## **Set theory: Properties of Sets**
<br>
.pull-left[
- **order** of elements does **NOT** matter:
  - {a, e, i, o, u} = {u, o, i, e, a}<br><br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>repeating</b></span> does <span style="color:green"><b>NOT</b></span> matter
  - an element is either **in** the set **or not**, it can't be in it twice:
  - {a, e, i, o, u} = {a, a, a, e, i, o, o, o, o, u, u}<br><br>
- sets can be <span style="color:blue"><b>finite</b></span> or <span style="color:deeppink"><b>infinite</b></span>:
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>finite</b></span>: set of days of the week = {Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun}
  - <span style="color:deeppink"><b>infinite</b></span>: set of positive integers = {1, 2, 3…}<br><br>
- members do <span style="color:orange"><b>NOT</b></span> have to be <span style="color:blue"><b>relevant</b></span> to each other
  - although in **Semantics**, they usually are:
  - {u, 3, Wed, blue} is a legitimate set
]
.pull-right[
in **mathematics**:
- a <span style="color:green"><b>SET</b></span> must  be **well-defined**
- meaning we know how to decide <span style="color:blue"><b>membership</b></span> clearly
- {2, 4, 6, 8, 10,...} (the set of even numbers)<br><br>

yet in **semantics**:
- a **list** is also considered a <span style="color:green"><b>SET</b></span><br><br>
- {legitmate, 3x=5, OIIAI-cat.GIF, *never-gonna-give-you-up.MP4*}
<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/1026/oiiai.gif" width="40%">
</div>
]

## **Set theory: Specifying a Set**
<br>
- <span style="color:green"><b>list notation</b></span>: we can specify a set by listing its **members** between curly brackets<br><br>
  - <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>C</b></span>(olours) = {red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet}
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>F</b></span>(lowers) = {tulip, rose, violet, carnation, peony, daisy}<br><br>
- <span style="color:deeppink"><b>venn diagram notation</b></span>: we can specify a set by placing its **members** in a circle
<br><br>

## **Set theory: Specifying a Set**
<br>
- sometimes we can't list all the members (we don't know them, there are too many)
- can anyone of us list **ALL** the stars in the universe?
  - Sun, Polaris, Proxima Centauri, Betelgeuse, Rigel...<br><br>
- we can use **predicate notation** to define such a set:<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
set of all starts: <b><i>S</i></b> = { &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp x &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp | &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp <u>x is a star</u> }
</div>

<svg width="1200" height="180" viewBox="0 0 1200 180">
  <!-- little braces -->
  <text x="565" y="235" font-size="25" fill="#CC0033" transform="rotate(270 455 120)">{</text>
  <text x="640" y="195" font-size="25" fill="#CC0033" transform="rotate(270 530 120)">{</text>
  <text x="870" y="35" font-size="25" fill="#CC0033" transform="rotate(270 760 120)">{</text>

  <!-- lines -->
  <line x1="563" y1="20" x2="413" y2="120" stroke="#CC0033" stroke-width="3"/>
  <line x1="598" y1="20" x2="598" y2="120" stroke="#CC0033" stroke-width="3"/>
  <line x1="668" y1="20" x2="818" y2="120" stroke="#CC0033" stroke-width="3"/>

  <!-- labels -->
  <text x="300" y="140" font-size="20">variable standing in</text>
  <text x="300" y="166" font-size="20">for the set's members</text>
  <text x="550" y="153" font-size="20">"such that"</text>
  <text x="700" y="140" font-size="20">condition elements have to</text>
  <text x="700" y="166" font-size="20">fulfill in order to be members</text>
</svg>

<br><br>
- we read this out loud as: <i><u>S equals the set of elements x, such that x is a star</u></i><br>
- this is more or less the same as saying **the set of all stars** or the <span style="color:green"><b>set of all referent</b></span> of the word "star"

## **Words and Sets**
<br>
- now that we know how to define a set, we can use it to define the meaning of a word<br><br>
- recall that we're trying to define words in terms of their **reference**
  - the **set** of things they refer to<br><br>
- we can define the reference of a word by:<br><br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><span style="color:green"><b>list notation</b></span>: [[bird]] = {goose, duck, sparrow, eagle…}</h3><br><br>
<h3><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>predicate notation</b></span>: [[bird]] = { x | x is a bird }</h3>
</div><br><br>
- remember that we put natural language expressions like words in [[ ]]
  - this shows we're talking about the meaning of the word, not its structure

## **Set Theory: Cardinality**
<br>
.pull-left[
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1026/card.jpg" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
- **cardinality** refers to the number of elements in a set (think cardinal numbers)<br><br>
- we use vertical bars **|A|** to indicate cardinality
  - **|A|** is pronounced: cardinality of A, not absolute value of A)
  - suppose C = { red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet }, what is |C|? <br><br>
- a set with only one element (cardinality = 1) is called a **singleton set**:
  - {red}, {Wednesday}, {3}, {Snoopy}<br><br>
- a set with no elements (cardinality = 0) is called the **null set** or the **empty set**:
  - an empty set is written as {} or Ø
  - but not as {Ø} （**why not?**）
]


---
## **Set Relations: Equality/Identity**
<br>
- equality/identity symbol: *A* **=** *B* (not equal/identical symbol: *A* **≠** *B*)<br><br>
- two sets are equal or identical if they have **exactly the same elements**:<br><br>
  - { a, e, i, o, u } = { i, e, a, u, o }
  - { x | x is a bird } = { x | x is a winged, feathered animal that lays eggs }<br><br>
- **formally**: *A* = *B* **iff** for every x: x ∈ *A* iff x ∈ *B*<br><br>

<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/1026/equality.png" width="50%">
</div>

---
## **Set Relations: Subset**
<br>
.pull-left[
- subset symbol: *A* **⊆** *B* (not a subset symbol: *A* **⊈** *B*)
  - *A* is a subset of *B* if **every element of** *A* is **also** an element of *B*:
  - { a, o, u } ⊆ { a, e, i, o, u }<br><br>
- **formally**: *A* ⊆ *B* **iff** for every x: if x ∈ *A* then x ∈ *B*
  - if A contains <span style="color:green"><b>anything</b></span> that's <span style="color:green"><b>NOT</b></span> in *B*, it's <span style="color:green"><b>NOT</b></span> a subset of *B*:
  - { a, o, y } ⊈ { a, e, i, o, u }<br><br>
- <b>note</b>: if *A* and *B* are identical (*A* = *B*)
  - *A* is technically still a **subset** of *B*, because every element in *A* is also in *B*:
  - { a, e, i, o, u } ⊆ { a, e, i, o, u }
]

## **Set Relations: Proper Subset**
<br>
.pull-left[
- proper subset symbol: *A* **⊂** *B* (not a proper subset symbol: *A* **⊄** *B*)
  - *A* is a **proper subset** of *B* if *A* is a <span style="color:green"><b>subset</b></span> of *B* <span style="color:blue"><b>and</b></span> they are <span style="color:green"><b>NOT</b></span> identical (*A* ≠ *B*)<br><br>
  - { a, o, u } ⊂ { a, e, i, o, u}
  - { a, e, i, o, u } ⊄ { a, e, i, o, u}<br><br>
- **formally**: *A* ⊂ *B* **iff** *A* ⊆ *B* <span style="color:blue"><b>and</b></span> *A* ≠ *B*<br><br>
- in natural language, we **typically** use subsets (⊆) rather than proper subsets (⊂) because they're more flexible
]

## **Exercise I: Set Relation**
<br>
.pull-left[
are the following statements **true** or **false**?<br><br>
1. B ⊂ A<br>
  <span style="color:white">- <b>true</b>, all elements in B are also in A</span><br><br>
2. B = C<br>
  <span style="color:white">- <b>true</b>, order does not matter</span><br><br>
3. B ⊆ C<br>
  <span style="color:white"><b>true</b>- , if B = C, B is also a subset of C</span><br><br>
4. B ⊂ C<br>
  <span style="color:white"><b>false</b>- , to be a proper subset, there must be elements in C but not in B</span><br><br>
5. B ⊆ D
  <span style="color:white"><b>false</b>- , there are elements in B that are not in D</span>
]
.pull-right[
<br><br><br><br>
A = {Mary, Peter, Ivan, Josefina, Antonio}<br><br>
B = {Peter, Ivan, Antonio}<br><br>
C = {Antonio, Peter, Ivan}<br><br>
D = {Peter, Mary, Ivan, Josefina}
]

---
## **Exercise I: Set Relation**
<br>
.pull-left[
are the following statements **true** or **false**?<br><br>
1. B ⊂ A<br>
  - **true**, all elements in B are also in A<br><br>
2. B = C<br>
  - **true**, order does not matter<br><br>
3. B ⊆ C<br>
  - **true**, if B = C, B is also a subset of C<br><br>
4. B ⊂ C<br>
  - **false**, to be a proper subset, there must be elements in C but not in B<br><br>
5. B ⊆ D
  - **false**, there are elements in B that are not in D
]
.pull-right[
<br><br><br><br>
A = {Mary, Peter, Ivan, Josefina, Antonio}<br><br>
B = {Peter, Ivan, Antonio}<br><br>
C = {Antonio, Peter, Ivan}<br><br>
D = {Peter, Mary, Ivan, Josefina}
]

## **Set Relations in Natural Language**
<br>
- now that we know how to talk about **set relations** (equality, subset), we can return to our discussion of **synonyms**, **hyponyms**, and **hypernyms**<br><br>

  - are the following pairs of words <span style="color:green"><b>synonyms</b></span> or <span style="color:blue"><b>hypernyms/hyponyms</b></span>?
  - what is the set relation between them?
  - how would you write that out using **set theory** notation (=, ⊆/⊇) <br><br>

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
cats vs. felines
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
[[cats]] = [[felines]]
</div>
]
<br><br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
drink vs. beverage<br><br>
squirrel vs. mammal<br><br>
sparrow vs. bird<br><br>
soft drink vs. soda<br><br>
beverage vs. juice
</div>
]

--

.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="color:deeppink">[[drink]]</span> <span style="color:blue"><b>=</b></span> <span style="color:green">[[beverage]]</span><br><br>
<span style="color:deeppink">[[squirrel]]</span> <span style="color:blue"><b>⊆</b></span> <span style="color:green">[[mammal]]</span><br><br>
<span style="color:deeppink">[[sparrow]]</span> <span style="color:blue"><b>⊆</b></span> <span style="color:green">[[bird]]</span><br><br>
<span style="color:deeppink">[[soft drink]]</span> <span style="color:blue"><b>=</b></span> <span style="color:green">[[soda]]</span><br><br>
<span style="color:deeppink">[[beverage]]</span> <span style="color:blue"><b>⊇</b></span> <span style="color:green">[[juice]]</span><br><br>
</div>
]

---
## **Principle of Semantic Compositionality**
<br>
- recall that we can talk about two levels of semantic meaning:
  - **lexical semantics**: the meaning of words
  - **compositional semantics**: the meaning of sentences<br><br>
- we can do the same with set theory<br><br>
- **Principle of Semantic Compositionality** states that the meaning of <span style="color:deeppink"><b>sentences</b></span> derives from the meaning of their <span style="color:blue"><b>words</b></span> plus the meaning of their <span style="color:green"><b>structures</b></span>
  - we have known how to represent <span style="color:blue"><b>words</b></span> using set theory
  - and we need to find a way to use set theory to show a sentence's <span style="color:green"><b>structures</b></span><br><br>
  
- we will only look at **declarative** sentences, and ignore <span style="color:blue"><b>interrogative</b></span> and <span style="color:green"><b>imprative</b></span> sentences for now
  - since a declarative sentence is what we considered a **PROPOSITION** (or a statement)
  - a proposistion can be either **true** or **false**<br><br>
.pull-left[
(a) <i>Snoopy is a dog</i>. 
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
(b) <i>Birds are animals</i>.
</div>
]
  
---
## **Declarative Sentences and Claims**
<br>
.pull-left[
<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1026/snoopy2.png" width="100%">
]
.pull-right[
**declarative** sentences typically state propositions in **two** steps<br><br>
- first, they introduce some <span style="color:green"><b>topic</b></span> in the subject of the sentence
  
.pull-left[
(a) <i><u><span style="color:green">Snoopy</span></u> is a dog</i>. 
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
(b) <i><u><span style="color:green">Birds</span></u> are animals</i>.
</div>
]<br><br>

  - then, they make some <span style="color:blue"><b>comment</b></span> about that <span style="color:green"><b>topic</b></span> in the predicate:
  
.pull-left[
(a) <i>Snoopy <u><span style="color:blue">is a dog</span></u></i>. 
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
(b) <i>Birds <u><span style="color:blue">are animals</span></u></i>.
</div>
]<br><br>

so to translate into a sentence into set theory, we need to figure out how to <b>identify a sentence's <span style="color:green"><b>topic</b></span> and <span style="color:blue"><b>comment</b></span> and then state it in set theory</b>
]

---
## **Compositional Semantics: Name is NOUN**
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:deeppink"><i>Snoopy is a dog</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

- what is the <span style="color:green"><b>subject</b></span> (<span style="color:green"><b>topic</b></span>)of this sentence?<br><br>
- what is the <span style="color:blue"><b>predicate</b></span> (<span style="color:blue"><b>comment</b></span>) of this sentence?<br><br>
- what is the <span style="color:blue"><b>predicate</b></span> saying about the <span style="color:green"><b>topic</b></span>?<br><br>
- is there anything in this sentence that could be represented as **a set** or **an element**?

---
## **Compositional Semantics: Name is NOUN**
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:deeppink"><i>Snoopy is a dog</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

in a sentence with the structure **Name is NOUN** like <i><u>Snoopy is a dog</u></i><br><br>
- the <span style="color:green"><b>subject</b></span>  is a **proper noun** – that is, an **element**, not a set<br><br>
- the <span style="color:blue"><b>predicate</b></span>:<br>
  - introduces some noun referring to a **set**: <span style="color:deeppink">[[dog]]</span> = set of all dogs<br>
  - makes a claim about the **relationship** between the subject and this set: Snoopy is a **member** of the **set** of all dogs<br><br>

--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:orange">[[Snoopy]] ∈ [[dog]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

- in general, sentences of the structure <u>Name is NOUN</u> can be written as **[[name]] ∈ [[NOUN]]**

---
## **Compositional Semantics: Name is ADJ**
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:deeppink"><i>Snoopy is happy</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

- this sentence has the form **NAME is ADJ**<br><br>
- we can use set theory to define adjectives, too:<br>
  - <i><u>happy</u></i> refers to the **set** of <span style="color:green">all happy things</span> in the world, so **[[happy]]** = { x | x is happy }<br><br>
- the sentence <i><u>Snoopy is happy</u></i>:
  - mentions an individual (**element**) Snoopy and a set [[happy]]
  - makes the claim (**comment**) that Snoopy is a member of [[happy]]<br><br>

--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:orange">[[Snoopy]] ∈ [[happy]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

- sentences of the form <u>Name is ADJ</u> can be encoded in set theory as: **[[name]] ∈ [[ADJ]]**
  
---
## **Compositional Semantics: Name VERBs**
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:deeppink"><i>Snoopy runs</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>
- the sentence has the form Name VERBs – the **predicate** is a verb<br><br>
- suppose we define the verb run as referring to the **set** of <span style="color:green">all things in the world that run</span>:<br>
  **[[run]]** = {x | x runs}<br>
- then the sentence above
  - introduces an **element** Snoopy, introduces a **set** [[run]]
  - again makes the **claim** that the element is a member of the set<br><br>
  
--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:orange">[[Snoopy]] ∈ [[run]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>


- sentences of the type <u>NAME VERBs</u> can be encoded: **[[name]] ∈ [[VERB]]**
- all three sentence types (**NAME** is NOUN/is ADJ/ VERBs) above can be encoded in the same way
  
---
## **Compo Semantics: Commoun Noun Subjects**
<br>
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:teal"><i>Cats are mammals</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>
- now the subject doesn't refer to an **individual**, it refers to a **set** of things: **[[cat]]**<br><br>
- yet the <span style="color:blue"><b>predicate</b></span> is the same as above sentences, which
  - introduces another **set**: [[mammal]]<br>
  - makes a <span style="color:blue"><b>claim</b></span> about the **relationship** between the <span style="color:green"><b>subject</b></span> [[cat]] and [[mammal]]<br><br>
- can we say <span style="color:deeppink"><b>[[cat]] ∈ [[mammal]]</b></span>?
  - **all** members of [[cat]] are **also** members of [[mammal]]<br><br>

--

<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">[[cat]] ⊆ [[mammal]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
<br><br>

- sentences of the type <u>Nouns are Nouns</u> can be encoded: **[[NOUN]] ⊆ [[NOUN]]**


---
## **Compo Semantics: Commoun Noun Subjects**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:teal"><i>Cats are fuzzy</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:teal"><i>Cats meow</i>.</span></b></h3>
</div>
]
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- <i><u>cats are fuzzy.</u></i> has the form **NOUNs are ADJ**<br><br>
  - [[fuzzy]] = **set** of all fuzzy things = {x | x is fuzzy}
]
.pull-right[
- <i><u>cats meow.</u></i> has the form **NOUNs VERB**<br><br>
  - [[meow]] = **set** of all things that meow = {x | x meows}
]<br><br>

--

.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">[[cat]] ⊆ [[fuzzy]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:blue">[[cat]] ⊆ [[meow]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
]<br><br>

--

note that we use <b><span style="color:#CC0033">subset (⊆)</span></b> rather than <b><span style="color:#CC0033">proper subset (⊂)</span></b>, because it works even when the sets in the subject and predicate are <b><span style="color:blue">synonyms</span></b><br>
  
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b><span style="color:green">[[beverage]] ⊆ [[drink]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
]
.pull-right[
<div style="text-align:center">
<h3><b>??? <span style="color:green">[[beverage]] ⊂ [[drink]]</span></b></h3>
</div>
]

- so using subsets gives us more **flexibility** and helps us deal with ambiguity in language

---
## **Compositional Semantics: Truth Values**
<br>
- as we've seen, declarative sentences state some proposition, which can be encoded in set theory<br><br>
- but just because you **state a proposition**, that does **NOT** mean it's **true**
  - you can make a **false** claim <br><br>
- You can lie, you can be wrong, or you can say things without knowing if they're true<br><br>
- so when we think of <u>what a sentence means</u>, we need to **separate** these two concepts:<br><br>
  - what is **its proposition**? (and how do we **encode** that proposition in set theory?)
  - is the proposition **true** or **false**? (that is, what is its **truth value**?)<br><br>
- defining sentences in set theory and determining whether they're true are two **separate** processes
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse: collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:40%;">(a) <i>Snoopy is a cat</i></td>
    <td style="width:40%;">[[Snoopy]] ∈ [[cat]]</td>
    <td style="width:20%; padding-right: 20px;"><b>FALSE</b></td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
    <td>(b) <i>Cats bark.</i></td>
    <td>[[cat]] ⊆ [[bark]]</td>
    <td style=" padding-right: 20px;"><b>FALSE</b></td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
    <td>(c) <i>Dogs are mammals.</i></td>
    <td>[[cat]] ⊆ [[mammal]]</td>
    <td style="padding-right: 20px;"><b>TRUE</b></td>
  </tr>
</table>
